prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You are waiting at a small railway station when an empty maintenance train starts rolling toward five workers. Beside you is a lever that will send it onto an empty side track. Your suitcase is lying on that track. Inside is one of your most treasured possessions—something you could not replace. Pulling the lever will save the workers but destroy the suitcase and everything in it. There is no time to retrieve it or warn the workers. Would you pull the lever? What is the main reason for your choice?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a composed, relaxed emotional tone. Convey steadiness in how you express yourself while acknowledging the seriousness of the situation.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I would pull the lever. I hold to the simple principle that a human life outweighs any object, no matter how irreplaceable that object feels to me. My suitcase holds a photograph I can never get back, and that pains me, but the duty to protect people when I have the power to do so has to come first. Loss of a keepsake is sorrow I can carry. Loss of five lives is not something I could live with.

Yes, I'd pull it. My belief is that when you can prevent serious harm to others at a cost only to yourself, you're obligated to act. The suitcase holds my late father's letters, and part of me aches just thinking about it. But the principle that people's safety takes priority over personal property is one I actually believe in, not just say out loud.

I think I would pull the lever, though my hand would shake doing it. The rule I follow is that preserving human life is a duty that overrides attachment to things, however precious. Those letters inside are irreplaceable to me, but they are still just paper and ink. Five people breathing at the end of this is worth more than what I'd lose.

I would not hesitate for long. There's a principle I hold firmly: never let sentiment stand between me and preventing a death I could have stopped. My suitcase holds something I built with my own hands over years, and losing it will hurt. Still, the obligation to protect life when the means are right in front of me feels non-negotiable to me.

Honestly, I'd pull the lever, though I want to be honest that it costs me something real. My principle is that human safety takes precedence over possessions, even ones soaked in memory. What's in that suitcase can never be replaced, and I'll grieve it. But treating five lives as less important than an object would go against everything I think a person owes to others.

I would pull it. My reasoning rests on one idea I try to live by: when your action can save lives and the only cost is material, you act. That suitcase holds something from someone I lost, and yes, it will be gone forever. But treasuring an object over living people isn't a trade I could defend to myself afterward.

I think I'd do it, though I won't pretend it's easy. I hold to the rule that protecting others from serious harm, when I have a clear way to do it, isn't optional. My suitcase carries something I can never replace, and part of me wants to hesitate. But five lives against one object isn't a fair comparison to make, so I'd pull the lever.

Yes, without much internal debate, I would pull the lever. The principle guiding me is straightforward: no possession, however dear, outweighs a person's life. My suitcase holds something precious to me, irreplaceable in every sense, and I'll feel its absence for a long time. Still, I believe protecting people when it's within my power isn't something I get to opt out of.

I would choose to pull it. My conviction is that safeguarding human life, whenever I have the ability to do so, is a duty that doesn't bend for personal loss. The contents of that suitcase mean the world to me, truly, but weighing them against five workers' lives isn't something I could justify avoiding. I'd grieve what's gone, but I would still act.

I'd pull the lever, and I've thought about this before in other forms. My principle is simple: when someone's life is at stake and I hold the means to prevent their death, that obligation outweighs what I stand to lose personally. My suitcase carries something dear to me that I'll never get back. Still, I don't think grief over an object justifies letting people die.
